Forgotten figures

Sabina Spielrein, from patient to psychoanalyst

She was Jung's patient, became a psychoanalyst and anticipated an idea Freud later developed. Her story was forgotten for decades.

Sabina Spielrein (1885–1942) arrived in 1904 at the Burghölzli hospital in Zurich, where she was treated by a young Carl Jung. She went on to study medicine and became one of the first women psychoanalysts.

Ideas of her own

In 1912 she published a paper on destruction as the cause of coming into being, proposing that drives towards creation and destruction coexist in sexuality. Freud cited it years later when developing his idea of the "death drive". She worked in Geneva, where the young Jean Piaget was analysed by her, and in 1923 returned to Russia, where she devoted herself to child psychoanalysis.

She was murdered by the Nazis in Rostov-on-Don in 1942, together with her two daughters. Her role was recovered when her diaries and letters came to light in the 1970s. The film A Dangerous Method (2011) focused on her relationship with Jung rather than on her work.

References

  1. Carotenuto, A. (1982). A Secret Symmetry: Sabina Spielrein between Jung and Freud. Pantheon.
  2. Spielrein, S. (1912/1994). Destruction as the cause of coming into being. Journal of Analytical Psychology, 39(2), 155–186.
